article.articleSummary:
- Bundibugyo virus, a filovirus closely related to Ebola, is driving a deadly outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda, with 695 confirmed cases and 138 deaths as of June 11, according to the WHO. The outbreak gained formal recognition after the death of a nurse. Bundibugyo causes severe hemorrhagic fever, marked by inflammation, vascular damage, bleeding, and multi-organ failure. Transmission occurs via direct contact with infected bodily fluids, placing health workers at high risk, especially in hospitals. Diagnosis is difficult because early symptoms resemble malaria and typhoid; laboratory confirmation is essential. In the DRC, limited local testing requires samples to travel to national reference labs, delaying confirmation and hindering isolation and contact tracing.

NPHIL conducted a nationwide assessment across 15 counties to appraise entry points, labs, and isolation facilities; surveillance cadres include 98 DSOs, 17 CSOs, and 22 ZSOs. Of 987 travelers screened—mostly returning from the Hajj in Saudi Arabia—966 completed 21 days of monitoring, with 21 under active follow-up and none symptomatic. The global outbreak totals 1,481 cases (1,460 DRC, 20 Uganda, 1 France), 454 deaths, and 229 recoveries (213 DRC, 16 Uganda). Liberia cites cross-border cooperation and World Bank support; a US$4.2 million Ebola preparedness budget is proposed.

The evaluation examined health centers’ buildings, equipment and staff, with a call to rapidly reinforce the response: the Obo isolation room and the hospital laboratory will be equipped to improve screening and patient care. A critical constraint is the shortage of qualified personnel—only four qualified health workers among about forty at Obo—with training planned and staff to be dispatched from Bangui. Insecurity and poor road conditions hinder movement; most interventions proceed by air. The UN, WHO and Institut Pasteur will deploy a mobile laboratory, specialists and a regular cargo flight for medicines and supplies.

article.articleHeadline: Le Point ISOS - "Hantavirus aboard a Dutch cruise ship: top priority. Ebola in five provinces of the Congo: silence"

Public health authorities, led by WHO/CDC, defined the incubation period, conducted contact tracing, and organized quarantines; subsequent cases were treated in specialized facilities. The incident highlighted the effectiveness of SARS-era lessons in cross-border management, with the WHO Director-General visiting the Canary Islands to destigmatize passengers. Media amplification contributed to a perceived crisis beyond epidemiology. Ebola in five provinces of Congo is described as not controlled, with population mobility driving cross-border spread, marking a shift from the earlier village-centered pattern seen in 2014 outbreaks in Guinea and Sierra Leone.

article.articleHeadline: Coltan and Ebola: The DRC bled dry, the world turns a blind eye
article.articleSummary: Eastern DRC is torn between M23 control of 15–30% of global coltan from Rubaya, North Kivu, financing its illegal administration since 2024, and a parallel Ebola outbreak in the west. Rwanda’s involvement remains disputed; US officials and the UN Security Council call for withdrawal of Rwandan forces per Resolution 2773. The Ebola crisis has over 2,000 laboratory-confirmed cases and 754 deaths, a fatality rate around 23.4%, with a funding gap of $70 million toward a $115 million need. Since July 2, three antiviral drugs are being tested as treatments; vaccines are not yet available. The international community faces a critical response to both resource-driven conflict and a severe health emergency, with thousands of Congolese lives at stake.

article.articleHeadline: Persistent itchy, dry eyes? Beware of Demodex mites taking up residence at the lash roots.
article.articleSummary: Demodex blepharitis with Meibomian Gland Dysfunction caused by Demodex mites at lash roots was diagnosed in a 32-year-old patient (alias Xiao Li) in Kunming, China. She had persistent itchy, dry eyes and tearing unresponsive to over-the-counter drops, with later conjunctival injection. Ocular surface testing revealed abundant Demodex and eggs, confirming Demodex blepharitis with Meibomian Gland Dysfunction. Demodex mites inhabit lash follicles and sebaceous and Meibomian glands; their secretions and waste can block glands, impair lipid secretion, and cause evaporative dry eye with itching, foreign body sensation, discharge and lash shedding. A four-cycle, in-hospital eradication plan was paired with anti-inflammatories and preservative-free artificial tears, plus daily home cleansing of lash roots with medical demodex swabs. Symptoms improved after the first course; final consolidation cleared the mites. Transmission can occur via direct/indirect contact; close contacts may need screening. Highlights: seek expert evaluation for persistent dry eye/itching; avoid indiscriminate antibiotics or steroids.

article.articleHeadline: Typhoon Bavi causes waterlogging in many parts of Liaoning; experts warn to prevent infection after wading through floodwater.
article.articleSummary: Typhoon Bavi-triggered flooding across Liaoning Province, China, left streets waterlogged. After wading, residents reported skin redness, itching, fever, and diarrhea. Shengjing Hospital experts warn floodwater is a polluted mix harboring bacteria (E. coli, Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Clostridium tetani, Leptospira), enteric viruses (norovirus, rotavirus), parasites (Cryptosporidium), and chemical pollutants (pesticides, heavy metals, oil). Prolonged exposure in sandals can breach the skin barrier, risking cellulitis or erysipelas and worsening fungal infections; pathogens may enter via hands to mouth or, in women, ascend to vaginitis or acute pelvic inflammatory disease. Flooded environments also contain feces and animal carcasses, increasing enteric, vector-borne, and zoonotic infections. Cleaning requires chlorine disinfection, boiling bed linens for 15 minutes, sun-drying non-wet fabrics, and thorough hand/skin hygiene. Seek medical care for diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, or skin/eye and gynecologic symptoms.

article.articleHeadline: Health services monitor 23,000 hepatitis B patients.
article.articleSummary: Macau SAR Health Services (SSM) monitor about 23,000 hepatitis B patients. By the end of last year, over 19,000 people were tested for the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), with more than 1,300 positives (roughly 6.8%). Since June this year, the minimum age for HBsAg testing without prior records was lowered from 50 to 40 years. Up to last month, 2,866 people were seen in Hepatology outpatient clinics. The Macau Health Survey 2026 has been completed, with preliminary results due by year-end. The 2016 survey estimated adult HBsAg positivity at 7.6% (about 34,000 infections), with around 4% cirrhosis and 2% liver cancer per 100 positives; roughly 70% were over 50. Vaccination of those born in the 1990s reduced positivity to about 2%; in 2025, HBs positivity in children under five was 0.03%, meeting WHO target ≤0.1%. The government will promote World Hepatitis Day with free, anonymous rapid HBs tests and coordinating referrals for treatment with the Social Welfare Institute.

article.articleHeadline: Parasites Are Causing Explosive Diarrhea to Surge. Here's How to Avoid The Worst Ones
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-07-15, a Cyclospora outbreak in the United States is concentrated in Michigan, with lettuce and salad greens as a suspected vector; a specific source has not been confirmed and officials caution against bagged salads. Produce should be washed or peeled; avoid "washed and ready to eat" labels when possible. Cyclospora infections can cause explosive diarrhea. Separately, a World Health Organization report in The Lancet estimates that foodborne parasites caused about 4,886,427 DALYs in 2021. Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) has the largest global burden, contracted from undercooked pork or contaminated vegetables; prevention includes thorough cooking and freezing pork (-10 C for 5 days) and minimizing fecal contamination. Clonorchis sinensis is common in Asia and Russia (China heavily affected), acquired from raw/undercooked fish. Toxoplasma gondii is widespread, risky for pregnant women; avoid cat litter. Other parasites include Cryptosporidium, Fasciola, Trypanosoma cruzi, and Ascaris; emphasize hygiene and safe water.

Chinese workers from Bureau 2 and Bureau 5 were given on-site guidance about plague—its early signs and its threat to humans—transmission pathways (through rodents and fleas, and by airborne droplets), and preventive hygiene measures. To ensure comprehension, leaflets were distributed in Chinese. The outreach is part of ongoing preventive efforts to safeguard against highly dangerous infections and maintain epidemiological stability in the region, the department said. article.articleSummary: After typhoon-induced floods and waterlogging in China, the China CDC warns of increased infectious-disease risk as floodwaters carry microbes from sewage, feces, and animal carcasses. Critical precautions include: drink only disinfected, boiled, or bottled water; avoid spoiled, moldy, or flood-contaminated foods; wash fruits and vegetables with clean water and keep raw and cooked foods separate to prevent enteric infections. Post-flood cleaning should remove mud, standing water, garbage, and animal remains; disinfect households and dining ware; maintain ventilation and dryness; check doors and screens, and use nets, mosquito coils, or repellents to prevent bites. In schistosomiasis-endemic areas, anyone with fever or diarrhea of unknown origin after flood exposure should seek prompt medical care. The guidance emphasizes prevention, environmental hygiene, and timely medical evaluation to curb outbreaks in the affected regions.

article.articleHeadline: 'Like in a horror movie': The brain-eating amoeba could spread around the world.
article.articleSummary: Naegleria fowleri, the brain-eating amoeba causing primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), spreads through nasal passages after swimming in warm freshwater. An 11-year-old boy, Jordan Smelski, died in Costa Rica seven and a half days after swimming, following headaches, vomiting, hallucinations and seizures. Globally, India reported over 200 PAM cases last year—the largest outbreak on record—with continued new cases, expanding concern beyond traditional lakes. From 1962–2023, about 488 cases were documented worldwide with around 97% mortality. Notable recent signals include Slovakia’s first case in 2025; cases in Minnesota, Taiwan (2023); and a US child who died after exposure at a contaminated pool surface. Climate warming may increase activity and extend habitats to Europe and East Asia. Children around age 12 are especially vulnerable. Early multi-drug regimens with anti-edema therapy can help, but survivors remain rare; the Kerala outbreak highlights shifting distribution.

article.articleHeadline: Summer peak! A painless, non-itchy "little black crust"—the culprit is this type of insect.
article.articleSummary: Scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi), transmitted by chigger mites, caused a lab-confirmed case in Nanjing, China. A 32-year-old man developed a week-long fever up to 40C, followed by a painless, non-itchy rash. A hidden eschar—the size of a fly on the scrotal area—led to targeted testing, with Orientia tsutsugamushi IgM positive. After treatment, fever subsided the next day, rash faded by day four, and the eschar gradually detached. The report emphasizes that scrub typhus can mimic viral illness; the concealed eschar is a key diagnostic clue on thorough skin examination. Transmission involves rodents as reservoirs and chigger mite bites, with a 5–20 day incubation. Prevention focuses on clearing grass and debris around living areas, wearing long sleeves and pants outdoors, and washing promptly afterward, especially in axilla, groin, and other skin folds.

article.articleHeadline: Girl with a fever for three days thought she had a cold; diagnosed with encephalitis; early symptoms were highly deceptive.
article.articleSummary: 12-year-old Xinxin in Zhengzhou, China, presented with three days of fever up to 40°C, sore throat, and marked lethargy. In the pediatric clinic of Zhengzhou People’s Hospital, involuntary movements of the hands, feet, and mouth prompted suspicion of encephalitis. EEG and MRI confirmed a diagnosis of viral encephalitis. After multidisciplinary treatment, Xinxin recovered and was discharged. The case underscores that pediatric viral encephalitis can mimic common colds in early stages, delaying treatment. Children’s developing immune systems and partially intact blood-brain barrier allow viruses—such as enteroviruses, herpesviruses, influenza, or mumps virus—to invade the central nervous system via respiratory or digestive routes, causing inflammation and edema of brain tissue. Parents should note fever with abnormal behavior, poor appetite, irritability, lethargy, and later signs like seizures or paralysis warrant urgent evaluation.

article.articleHeadline: Dangerous tick-borne viruses can outsmart the human immune system
article.articleSummary: Five brand-new human-infecting tick-borne viruses identified in the last decade include three in China, one in Japan, and one in California. The best-known is Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus, which kills more than one-third of those it infects. A standout among the newly described viruses is Pacific Coast tick nairovirus, found in ticks in California and responsible for the strongest suppression of human immune alarms observed to date. All of these viruses encode an OTU protein that removes host warning signals, undermining ubiquitin and ISG15–mediated responses at multiple steps. About 60% of California ticks carried Pacific Coast tick nairovirus, and the same ticks transmit Rocky Mountain spotted fever. The virus could be circulating undetected in people, potentially causing mild flu-like symptoms. Computer-based predictions of threat level were about 50% accurate overall, 82% for a well-studied virus.

The effort targets Aedes aegypti, the vector for these arboviruses. Up to July 4, 2026, 6,108,007 property inspections and 848,047 potential breeding deposits were treated or eliminated. Educational actions by the Municipal Health Secretariat stress public participation; residents can request inspections or report breeding sites via Central 1746 to support prevention.

article.articleHeadline: Santo André and Diadema report new mpox cases, and the region totals four cases.
article.articleSummary: Mpox (monkeypox) in the Grande ABC, São Paulo, totals four confirmed cases in 2026—Santo André with three, Diadema with one (woman, 50–54). Santo André reported nine suspected cases this year, with three confirmations and six exclusions; Diadema’s patient profile was not publicly disclosed. Last year the region had 27 mpox notifications. In 2022, São Paulo state recorded 4,283 mpox confirmations and 3 deaths, with Grande ABC totaling 220 cases and no fatalities; the first regional case in 2022 was a 36-year-old Santo André resident who had returned from Europe. State data for 2026 show 149 mpox cases in São Paulo and 356 in Brazil. Experts say the outbreak is not more aggressive than four years ago; transmission is mainly via direct contact with skin lesions, with fever, headache, myalgias, back pain, apathy, and lymphadenopathy as possible symptoms. Most cases are self-limiting; severe cases may require medications not routinely available in Brazil, but imported by SUS when needed. Virus is expected to clear after recovery.

article.articleHeadline: El Niño threatens to increase disease incidence and overwhelm health facilities in Mato Grosso.
article.articleSummary: El Niño intensification is forecast to persist into early 2027, driving higher temperatures, drought, and smoke in Mato Grosso, Brazil, with initial impacts seen in Várzea Grande as respiratory complaints surge—primarily influenza-like illness, allergic reactions, and worsening chronic lung disease. The climate conditions may expand circulation of respiratory infections, arboviruses (dengue, Zika, chikungunya, malaria), and waterborne diseases (cholera), increasing demand on the public health system with more consultations, tests, medications, and hospitalizations, especially among children, the elderly, and those with chronic illnesses. PAHO issued alerts for Latin America on climate-related health risks; air quality concerns stem from wildfires and smoke amid low humidity, elevating asthma, bronchitis, rhinitis, and cardiovascular admissions. Preventive actions include influenza vaccination (available at 25 basic health units in Várzea Grande for priority groups), hydration, nasal saline lavage, humidification, reducing dust and smoke exposure, cleaning with damp cloths, and eliminating Aedes aegypti breeding sites.

article.articleHeadline: What is avian influenza? Learn the symptoms, risks for humans and agriculture | CNN Brasil
article.articleSummary: Avian influenza A(H5N1) re-emerged since 2020, spreading among wild birds, farms across Europe, Americas, Asia and Oceania, Australia and New Zealand. Human risk remains low; cases are rare and linked to intense contact with infected birds or contaminated environments, with no sustained human-to-human transmission, and cooked poultry is not shown to transmit the virus. Migratory waterfowl are the main reservoirs; farm spread occurs through contact with infected birds, feces, secretions, water, feed, equipment, vehicles, or contaminated materials. In poultry, sudden death is characteristic; other signs include respiratory symptoms, reduced egg production, and swollen, purplish combs or wattles, plus leg hemorrhages. Protocols require isolation, culling, disinfection, and enhanced surveillance, and can trigger import suspensions on poultry products. Brazil detections began in 2023 in wild birds; in May 2025 a farm in Montenegro, Rio Grande do Sul, confirmed H5N1, triggering culling, decontamination, monitoring, and later lifting export restrictions as surveillance stayed clear.

article.articleSummary: Malaria risk rises in Manaus, Brazil, as the Amazonian summer begins, with increased use of bathing spots, igarapés, and rural sites. The Manaus City Hall, via the Municipal Health Secretariat (Semsa), reports Anopheles mosquitoes thriving during river recession, elevating cases from June through September. Manaus has recorded 3,284 malaria cases from January through June this year. The municipal network operates 55 diagnostic points in urban and rural areas to enable rapid testing and early treatment. Malaria is curable but can become severe if diagnosis and treatment are delayed or interrupted. Public health guidance emphasizes personal protection: repellents, long-sleeved clothing, bed nets, and avoiding exposure in forests, rivers, and igarapés during peak mosquito activity at dawn and late afternoon. Semsa maintains vector surveillance and control in high-risk zones and urges vigilance for symptoms such as fever, chills, headaches, and malaise.

article.articleSummary: Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis (Cfv) causes bovine genital Campylobacteriosis, a venereal disease contributing to reproductive losses in natural-service herds. In Brazil, 44 heifers were allocated to four groups: G1 vaccine A, G2 vaccine B, G3 infected with placebo, G4 negative control. After intravaginal challenge with Cfv, animals were followed for 105 days. Culture of vaginal-cervical mucus showed lower positivity in vaccinated groups (G1 61.81%, G2 45.45%) versus G3 87.27% (p<0.05). Local IgA and systemic IgG responses were detected by ELISA in all challenged groups, with earlier increases in G1/G2. Agglutinating antibodies were observed post-vaccination, strongest in G2 (p=0.0316). qPCR indicated a lower bacterial load in vaccinated cattle during sampling. Conclusion: vaccines yielded significantly earlier clearance of Cfv from the reproductive tract, associated with elevated early humoral responses; vaccines merit field evaluation to assess reproductive performance.

article.articleSummary: Dengue fever is increasingly common in the Asia-Pacific region, with significant impact on children as schools reopen. In Jakarta, prevention hinges on avoiding mosquito bites, recognizing early dengue symptoms, and knowing when to see a doctor. UNICEF explains that Aedes aegypti mosquitoes bite mainly during the day, with the highest risk about two hours after sunrise and before sunset. Transmission risk rises around homes, schools, workplaces, or routes with standing water, since Aedes aegypti can breed in even tiny amounts of water. Common breeding sites include buckets, discarded tires, puddles, or bottle caps. Most infections cause mild symptoms or none and recover in 1–2 weeks; roughly one in four people develop symptoms. Early recognition and timely medical care are crucial for protecting children during the school year.

article.articleHeadline: Risk of eating undercooked eggs, beware of diarrhea!
article.articleSummary: Indonesia warns that undercooked eggs can carry Salmonella, causing salmonellosis. Eggs may be contaminated before reaching consumers; eating partially cooked or raw eggs risks foodborne illness. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, fever, chills, and malaise, typically starting 12–36 hours after ingestion and lasting several days to a week. Vulnerable groups—children, the elderly, pregnant women, and those with weakened immune systems or chronic diseases—should avoid raw or undercooked eggs unless pasteurized. Pasteurized eggs, heated to kill bacteria without fully cooking, are safer for recipes needing raw eggs. Practical advice: choose clean, crack-free shells; refrigerate; cook until both white and yolk are firm; use pasteurized eggs for raw preparations; wash hands and utensils after handling raw eggs. Despite benefits, avoiding undercooked eggs protects public health in Indonesia.

article.articleHeadline: From smartphones to clinics: What Indonesia can learn from Thailand's disease tracking
article.articleSummary: COVID-19 spurred health-digital investments in Southeast Asia. Thailand’s integrated surveillance—more than 10,000 COVID-19 labs and a nationwide system linking local and central authorities—tracked outbreaks including among migrant workers. Mid-2025 COVID wave: roughly 374,000 cases and 84 deaths. Thailand’s early leadership in 2020 also showed strong results: 3,195 confirmed infections with 3,072 recoveries (96%). The Centre for COVID-19 Situation Administration (CCSA) coordinated across ministries, and public compliance with health measures was high (mask-wearing and hygiene 89–98% in a 2020 Imperial College London survey). Digital tools MorChana (GPS/Bluetooth for contacts) and MohPromt (digital vaccination records/EHRs) serve about 36 million users, enabling real-time test reporting and accessible records, including migrants. Indonesia built 600+ labs (2020–2021) and many health apps, but fragmentation persists (SatuSehat plus local Pikobar, Sawarna, PaPa Sulbar). Net Pracharat and Universal Coverage help; Indonesia should boost connectivity, regional integration, and public trust.

article.articleHeadline: Garbage piling up along the irrigation canal bank... Infectious disease danger near Thanjavur!
article.articleSummary: As of 15 July 2026, in Thanjavur district along the Muthalai-Muthuvar Irrigation Canal bank, illegal dumping of plastics, household waste, broken glass bottles and cow dung has surged, with waste often burned, releasing smoke and air pollution. The canal serves thousands of acres across Ramanathapuram, Pillaiyanatham, Kalimedu and Chakrasamanthan villages, providing irrigation water for rice, sugarcane and banana crops. Burning waste and stagnant litter raise concerns about air and water pollution, soil fertility decline, and potential health hazards for nearby residents, including dengue, malaria and chikungunya due to increased mosquito breeding. Farmers and residents demand immediate cleanup, strict enforcement with fines, monitoring cameras, warning boards, and awareness campaigns. Authorities at district and panchayat levels are urged to act promptly to protect agriculture, environment, and public health.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue, Typhoid, or Leptospirosis? Doctors Warn These Diseases Can Look Alarmingly Similar
article.articleSummary: Dengue, leptospirosis, and typhoid can begin with indistinguishable symptoms during the monsoon season, complicating early diagnosis. Overlapping presentations include fever, headache, body aches, fatigue, nausea, and appetite loss, making reliance on symptoms alone insufficient. Mumbai-based Dr. Niranjan Patil of Metropolis Healthcare Limited warns that delays in correct diagnosis and treatment can occur without timely testing. Timely diagnostic testing is essential because each disease has a different cause and requires a different treatment approach. While the diseases share symptoms, their infectious agents and management differ, underscoring the need for laboratory confirmation to guide therapy and avoid mismanagement. The report does not provide case counts or outbreak figures.

article.articleHeadline: Fever outbreak on the rise in the state; eight deaths in Ernakulam alone in two weeks.
article.articleSummary: July 15, 2026: Kerala faces rising fever outbreaks. In Ernakulam, July has seen 10,050 fever cases so far, with eight deaths in the past two weeks. Dengue activity is up, with 262 cases treated in the last 13 days; Kalamasheri accounts for 51 dengue cases since July 1 (18 on July 1; five the next day; 12 last Sunday), with cases also reported in Aluva, Kakkanad, Binanipuram, Cherunni, Chottanikkara, Idappilly, Kadavanthra, Thrikkakara and Edappilly. Monkeypox (elippani) totals 19 cases with seven deaths; a 23-year-old interstate migrant worker from Kadavanthra died. In June, deaths (27 district-wide) were driven by influenza, West Nile, and H1N1, with 11 deaths due to monkeypox. Monkeypox symptoms include fatigue, leg pains, headache, fever, and abdominal pain; prevention emphasizes hygiene, avoiding soil/contact exposure, timely treatment, and, where advised, prophylaxis for high-risk workers.

triage.headline_ja: 州内で発熱の発生が増加、エルナークラム郡だけで2週間に8人死亡

article.articleHeadline: Like in a Horror Movie: The Brain-Eating Amoeba Could Spread Worldwide.
article.articleSummary: Naegleria fowleri, the brain-eating amoeba, caused the death of 11-year-old Jordan in Costa Rica after swimming at a hotel’s thermal spring; he developed severe headache, vomiting, confusion, seizures and died seven days post-exposure from primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), a nearly always fatal brain infection. In India, last year (2025) recorded over 200 cases—the largest global outbreak to date, with fewer than 500 cases historically. The parasite is emerging in new regions, including Slovakia (first case in 2025), Minnesota (USA), and Taiwan (2023) at an indoor surfing facility; a US child died in 2023 after exposure at a splash-pad. Warmer waters from climate change are expanding habitats beyond lakes and rivers, increasing risk for mostly children (average around 12). Since 1962–2023, about 488 cases worldwide with ~97% fatal. Early detection may allow multi-drug treatment, though outcomes remain poor.

triage.headline_ja: ホラー映画のように：脳を食うアメーバが世界的に広がる可能性
triage.triage_reason: インドで2025年に200例超という過去最大規模のNaegleria fowleri感染アウトブレイクが記録されており、致死率97%と極めて深刻。IHR基準（深刻な公衆衛生影響、異常性）に2つ該当するため。
triage.notes: Naegleria fowleriは水系（温水環境）由来の感染症でヒト-ヒト感染はしない。記事は複数国（コスタリカ、スロバキア、米国、台湾）での事例を挙げているが、対象国リストに該当するのはインドのみ。インドでの2025年の200例超という記録的規模のアウトブレイクは注視が必要。気候変動による生息域拡大が指摘されている点も継続的モニタリングの根拠となる。

article.articleHeadline: Indore Shishukunj School Food Poisoning: The shocking truth behind 150 children falling ill! Dangerous bacteria found in the school's water, and the ice cream report also left everyone stunned.
article.articleSummary: Indore Shishukunj School in Indore district, Madhya Pradesh, faced a mass food-poisoning event on June 20, with about 150 students developing vomiting and diarrhea. Laboratory findings revealed multiple contamination sources: the school water tested positive for coliform bacteria (the same type implicated in the Bhagirathpura incident); soybean oil and a salted snack sample also failed. Ice cream samples were found to harbor Listeria bacteria, with the ice cream test completely failing. In response, district authorities formed a special investigation team and ordered the school kitchen sealed to prevent further exposure. Food Officer Manish Swami confirmed the findings. The article does not report any fatalities. This incident highlights food safety risks in school canteens and related food items, prompting immediate public health actions.

article.articleHeadline: 115 children fall ill, 12 hospitalised after eating water balls in Rajasthan village
article.articleSummary: In Polai Khurd village, Kota district, Rajasthan, 115 children fell ill after consuming pani-patasi (water balls), with 12 admitted to the Community Health Centre in Simliya and others treated at a village medical camp. Symptoms included vomiting, diarrhoea, and stomach pain, with illness onset reported from Tuesday night. Health officials dispatched two medical teams and 108 ambulance services; a special medical camp was established as door-to-door surveys by ANMs and ASHAs sought additional cases. Most patients are stable. The pani-patasi vendor is reportedly from nearby Sholi village. The Food Safety Department collected samples of ingredients, chutneys, and water; source water samples were sent for laboratory analysis. Laboratory results are pending, and findings will guide action against those responsible and future prevention.

article.articleHeadline: Kangra to conduct study on TB burden, disease hotspots - The Tribune
article.articleSummary: 14 TB-related deaths in Q2 2026 in Kangra district per the District TB Death Audit under NTEP, with deaths mainly linked to advanced co-morbidities and non-TB causes. Deputy Commissioner Hemraj Bairwa directs strengthening critical care and a district-wide study to map TB burden, hotspots, and vulnerable groups to accelerate elimination. Referral centers at Civil Hospitals Nurpur, Palampur, Dehra; Zonal Hospital Dharamsala; and Dr Rajendra Prasad Government Medical College, Tanda, will handle critically ill TB cases. Emphasis on early diagnosis, prompt hospitalization, and integrated management of diabetes, hypertension, chronic respiratory diseases, and malignancies; intensive home-based follow-up and regular monitoring; expanded palliative care. Programs include TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyan 2.0, Universal Drug Susceptibility Testing, TB preventive treatment, Nikshay Mitra, community screening, and Ayushman Aarogya Shivirs for integrated TB/NCD screening.

article.articleHeadline: Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease in Children: Complications Parents Should Not Take Lightly
article.articleSummary: Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD) primarily affects children in Vietnam; most cases resolve in 7–10 days with mild symptoms. It is caused by enteroviruses, especially Coxsackievirus A16 and Enterovirus 71 (EV71). Transmission occurs via the digestive tract, respiratory secretions, saliva, vesicle fluid, and contaminated objects. Common symptoms include fever, sore throat, poor appetite, mouth ulcers, and vesicular rashes on the palms, soles, knees, or buttocks. Although usually mild, some children develop severe complications affecting the central nervous system and other organs. Urgent care is needed for warning signs such as fever ≥39°C or fever >48 hours, frequent startle responses, tremors, persistent irritability, restlessness, altered consciousness, repeated vomiting, rapid or labored breathing with chest retractions, cyanosis of lips or extremities, cold hands/feet, or unusually rapid heartbeat. Prevention relies on hygiene: handwashing, cleaning toys and surfaces, cooking foods thoroughly, avoiding contact with sick children, and monitoring outbreaks per Ministry of Health guidance in Hanoi, Vietnam (as of 15 July 2026).

article.articleHeadline: Life-threatening meningitis and acute cerebral edema after eating raw pork blood dish
article.articleSummary: Streptococcus suis meningitis with cerebral edema in a 45-year-old man from Bac Ninh, Vietnam, after eating a raw pork blood dish. Four days after ingestion he developed high fever, severe headache, nausea, progressing to altered consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale 9). Acute meningitis diagnosed; he required intubation, mechanical ventilation, antibiotics, and measures to control cerebral edema. After four days of intensive care his condition improved, extubated, and transferred to the Infectious Diseases ward for monitoring. Streptococcus suis is a leading cause of meningitis in Vietnamese adults and can cause septicemia with purpura, coagulopathy, septic shock, and multi-organ failure, with high mortality if treatment is delayed. Many cases occur even when patients deny pork products due to contamination from pork blood mixed to thicken dishes. Public health guidance emphasizes fully cooked foods and seeking medical care if fever or headache after consuming raw foods. Source: National Institute of Infectious and Tropical Diseases.

article.articleHeadline: Ha Tinh Province accelerates health checkups for the entire population, proactively preventing and controlling disease outbreaks.
article.articleSummary: Ha Tinh Province, Vietnam, in early 2026 intensified free health screenings, with over 609,000 residents checked by July 15, 2026, reaching 45.63% of the annual target. Dengue cases total 163 with two outbreaks accounting for 103 cases; hand, foot, and mouth disease 97; measles 12; meningococcal disease 1; pertussis 4; mumps 338; chickenpox 127; diarrhea 407; imported malaria 5; influenza 4,173. Hypertension and diabetes care continue under a family medicine model. Expanded immunization program vaccination coverage for children under 1 year in the first half of 2026 exceeded 46.5%. Bed occupancy reached 117%. Collaboration with Hanoi Medical University doctors provides on-site support and training. Sixteen communes/wards conducted periodic health checks and 28 communes/wards conducted screening. The province aims to expand high-tech services and achieve 100% population health screening in 2026, with strengthened early outbreak surveillance.

article.articleHeadline: Don't be complacent about the risk of Ebola entering.
article.articleSummary: Ebola risk entering Vietnam remains low, but Thanh Hoa Health Department intensifies surveillance at the international Na Meo Border Gate and Nghi Son Port. No Ebola cases in Vietnam to date. The MOH has urged authorities to remain vigilant at borders, communities, and healthcare facilities to quickly detect, isolate, and manage suspected cases. Thanh Hoa CDC's International Health Quarantine Division conducts routine health surveillance of people, vehicles, goods, and seafarers; tracks travel history from outbreak areas; and updates measures according to WHO guidance and MOH directives. Preparedness includes stocking equipment, disinfectants, PPE, and training for handling suspected cases, with ongoing multi-agency coordination with border guards, customs, and port authorities. Travelers from outbreak regions should monitor health for 21 days and seek care if fever, headache, muscle pain, fatigue, diarrhea, vomiting, or hemorrhagic signs occur. Early detection and rapid response are emphasized to prevent importation.

article.articleHeadline: Kanyemba Clinic upgrade boosts outbreak readiness
article.articleSummary: Zimbabwe upgrades Chapoto Clinic in Kanyemba, Mashonaland Central, into a rural hospital to improve local healthcare access and bolster cross-border outbreak readiness, including Ebola, in a border district near Zambia and Mozambique that handles travellers from across the sub-region. Chapoto Clinic, together with Mvurwi Hospital, has been designated as Ebola isolation and treatment centers; activating them would suspend normal services to manage cases. Preparedness measures include infection prevention and control training for health workers, stockpiled medicines and PPE, and a UNDP-funded on-site pharmacy. Gaps persist: unreliable water supply, inadequate accommodation and office space, ambulance shortages for referrals to Chitsungo, and a need for at least four non-contact thermal screening cameras (about US$4,000 each). A borehole site is identified, and border surveillance has been strengthened with environmental health officers and expanded community monitoring.

article.articleHeadline: Hog deaths in Negros Occidental 'under control' amid ASF outbreak
article.articleSummary: ASF outbreak in Negros Occidental remains under control as of July 13, 2026, with 14 localities affected and nine confirming ASF-positive cases. A total of 2,185 pigs have died across the 14 localities due to various swine diseases, representing 3.53% of the 61,854-strong hog population. Gov. Eugenio Jose Lacson said on July 14 that despite the deaths, the mortality is low and the situation is manageable, but warned against complacency. He attributed the containment to ongoing protocols and border controls designed to prevent ASF spread and urged continued vigilance. The report emphasizes the outbreak status as still under control, underscoring the need to maintain surveillance, biosecurity, and adherence to containment measures to avert a broader impact in Negros Occidental.

article.articleHeadline: Imus City steps up anti-dengue drive amid over 250 reported cases
article.articleSummary: As of July 15, 2026, Imus City, Cavite, has 259 dengue cases (180 confirmed, 42 probable, 37 suspected), down from 263 on July 1 (180 confirmed, 44 probable, 39 suspected). Dengue is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes; symptoms include high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, muscle/joint pain, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, and rashes, with severe cases causing persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, bleeding, blood in excretions, or breathing difficulties. Early diagnosis and prompt treatment are critical to prevent complications and deaths. The City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (CDRRMO) is intensifying measures to eliminate breeding sites and urges daily 4 p.m. search-and-destroy activities to remove stagnant water, aligning with peak Aedes activity. The DOH has promoted the '4 o'clock habit' nationwide since 2013 to curb dengue during the rainy season.

article.articleHeadline: 'Results of ASF vaccine trials still under close scrutiny' | Carmel Pedroza and Ada Pelonia
article.articleSummary: ASF vaccine trials in Cebu City remain under a controlled government program; the anti-ASF vaccine exists but is not licensed for commercial distribution and is overseen by the Bureau of Animal Industry. FDA approval is needed, requiring trial data on safety and efficacy. Ongoing results show antibodies in vaccinated pigs decline after about five months, and viral fragments were detected in urinary and intestinal tracts, raising environmental contamination concerns with biosecurity. The vaccine is therefore not yet recommended for widespread commercial use, especially among backyard and smallholder farms. There is no commercially available anti-ASF vaccine in the Philippines; rollout will continue under national guidelines with selected areas and participants, pending further data. Separately, BAI reports highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 in Pangasinan backyard poultry; initial case confirmed May 22 (ADDRL), with additional nearby cases. Measures include culling, disposal, cleaning/disinfection, movement control, and intensified monitoring. Properly cooked poultry and eggs are safe.

article.articleHeadline: Libya expands livestock restrictions to contain foot-and-mouth disease and protect the national livestock wealth - Libya News 24
article.articleSummary: Foot-and-mouth disease triggers a swift, nationwide preventive response in Libya as confirmed infections and suspected cases rise across western, eastern, and southern regions. Western Libya closes livestock markets and tightens movement controls: Mislatah district; Tarhouna’s Sidi al-Said market suspended; Qasr al-Akhiyar restricted; Sirte and Tripoli bolster surveillance and restrict transfers. In the east, markets in Sluq and Qmines are shut; Tobruk and Shahat curb livestock movement and market activity; Derna urges herd isolation after suspected cases in Qandula and Marawa in the Green Mountain. In the south, Ojla and Ubari close markets with 10–20 day movement limits; Tosh market is halted. Ongoing field surveillance, sampling, and laboratory testing accompany these measures to curb spread. Officials cite vaccination campaign irregularities and limited resources, underscoring a need to reinforce vaccination, monitoring, and rapid response to protect livestock and food security.

article.articleHeadline: "About 45 people contract HIV every day in Ghana": President of AIDS network says
article.articleSummary: Ghana records about 45 new HIV infections daily, per the Ghana HIV and AIDS Network (GHANET). Women account for roughly 68.5% of new infections and men 31.5%. GHANET President Ernest Amoabeng Ortsin ties the higher female share to factors including antenatal HIV testing and protection for the child, while noting many men do not seek hospital care. He also cites data suggesting most Ghanaian men have seven to nine sexual partners annually, which facilitates unprotected transmission. He underscores the need for intensified awareness, prevention, and support. Social media reactions call for renewed national campaigns and broader PrEP/PEP awareness, plus stronger action from the National AIDS Commission to curb rising infections.
